domains.title: Sacred Land of the Kumano Sanzan
domains.subtitle: Mountains, Pilgrimage, and Imperial Protection
domains.lead: Kumano is a mountainous region on the Kii Peninsula that has been sacred for over a thousand years. Its three great shrines — the Kumano Sanzan — drew emperors, aristocrats, and commoners on pilgrimage along the Kumano Kodō. Kumano is a place where dense forest, rushing rivers, and waterfalls create a landscape felt to be inhabited by powerful kami and Buddhas.

mythology.lead: Kumano's mythology blends imperial foundation legends, mountain asceticism, and the worship of waterfalls and forests.

myths.title: Yatagarasu and Emperor Jimmu
myths.text: When Emperor Jimmu, the first emperor, was lost in the mountains of Kumano, the sun goddess sent Yatagarasu, a three-legged crow, to guide him. The crow led Jimmu's army to victory and established the imperial line in Yamato. Yatagarasu remains a symbol of divine guidance and Kumano's protection of the nation.

myths.title: Mountain Asceticism
myths.text: Kumano became a center of Shugendō, the tradition of mountain asceticism that blends Shinto, Buddhism, and shamanic practice. Yamabushi practitioners walked the Kumano Kodō, performed rituals at waterfalls, and sought visions in the forest. The mountains were understood as a realm where kami and Buddhas met.

myths.title: Retired Emperors and Aristocrats
myths.text: From the 11th century onward, retired emperors and aristocrats made repeated pilgrimages to Kumano, sometimes dozens of times. These journeys were acts of devotion, politics, and spectacle, reinforcing the ties between the imperial house and the sacred mountains.

lore.syncretism: Kumano is a classic case of shinbutsu shūgō, the medieval fusion of Shinto and Buddhism. The Kumano shrines housed Buddhist temples, and the kami were identified with Buddhist divinities. The region also absorbed Shugendō practices, making it a threefold meeting ground of kami worship, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. The Meiji separation of Shinto and Buddhism stripped away the Buddhist layers, but the landscape retains its hybrid memory.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Kumano Kodō and Kii mountain shrines were designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2004. Modern pilgrims continue to walk the ancient routes, and Kumano remains a powerful symbol of spiritual journey in Japan. The three-legged crow appears on the logo of the Japan Football Association, tracing its lineage back to Jimmu's guide.
lore.extendedMeditation: Kumano asks us to walk. The pilgrimage is not a metaphor but a practice: each step through the forest is a step away from ordinary life and toward encounter. The crow, the waterfall, and the cedar grove are not scenery; they are participants in the journey.

lore.archaeology: The Kumano Sanzan (Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, Kumano Nachi Taisha) and the Kumano Kodō pilgrimage routes preserve a landscape of shrines, stone pavements, ritual sites, and Nachi Falls. Archaeological and architectural study documents the region's importance from the Heian period onward.
